China Lifts Temporary Export Ban on Construction Materials, Easing Pressure on Industry

China’s Ministry of Commerce announced yesterday that it has lifted a temporary ban on the export of several key construction materials, ending a three-week disruption that had stoked concerns across the sector. The measure, which was imposed in mid-May amid concerns over domestic supply levels and price volatility, had halted outbound shipments of products including cement, reinforced steel bars, and glass panels.

The abrupt halt in exports impacted a number of major producers, among them Ningxia Building Materials Group Co Ltd, which is a leading supplier for overseas infrastructure projects. The ban, industry executives said, led to a backlog of materials at ports and prompted some international contractors to delay timelines or seek alternative suppliers.

“The export suspension created a significant bottleneck for us,” said Zhang Wei, Deputy General Manager at Ningxia Building Materials Group Co Ltd. “We had orders awaiting shipment to Southeast Asia and the Middle East, and the uncertainty made it difficult to fulfill contractual commitments.”

The China Building Materials Federation, a trade association, estimated that the ban affected nearly 18% of the sector’s monthly export volume. “Some enterprises faced inventory pressure, while others saw cash flow constraints due to unshipped orders,” said Liu Rong, a senior analyst at the federation.

The government cited stabilization of domestic prices and improved inventory levels as the main reasons for lifting the restriction. A Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said in a briefing, “We have observed a rebalancing of supply and demand in the domestic market. The conditions that prompted the temporary measure no longer exist, allowing us to resume normal trade flows.”

Following the announcement, operations at affected companies quickly returned to normal. “We resumed export processing within 24 hours of the notice,” said Li Jun, export manager at Shandong Construction Materials Co, another leading player in the sector. “Although we lost some business during the ban, we are now working overtime to meet delayed orders.”

Industry observers expect the sector to recover quickly from the disruption, though some warn that repeated policy shifts could undermine foreign buyers’ confidence. “Restoring reliability is now the priority,” said Chen Ming, an independent trade policy consultant. “The speed of the government’s response has helped, but companies will need time to rebuild trust with overseas partners.”

With the embargo lifted and export activities back on track, construction material suppliers across China are now focused on clearing backlogs and restoring delivery schedules to pre-ban levels.
